paras: The attempted lynching of Antonio de Ritta took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the evening of October 26, 1882, when a crowd of Italian neighbors seized de Ritta, a Sicilian rag-picker, after a 7-year-old boy was shot dead in the yard of their Almond Street row. A police officer got him away from the crowd by locking him inside a street alarm box until a patrol wagon arrived, and a coroner's jury later held him for the boy's murder.

De Ritta, described as about sixty years old, lived with his wife next door to the boy's family in an old brick row on the south side of Almond Street between Third and Fourth streets. According to the wire report, circumstances suggested he shot the boy believing the child had stolen a pistol from his room.

Just after 6 o'clock, after dark, a pistol shot brought the residents out, and they found the boy, printed as Barbato Urbano, dying near the kitchen door of 318 Almond Street. His grandmother ran into the yard, denounced de Ritta, and tried to hold him, and she said he struck at her with a knife before she let go. De Ritta and his wife said a revolver had been stolen from them that morning, that the boy was the thief, and that he died when it went off by accident.

A crowd of Italian men and women surrounded him, and after the boy's 5-year-old brother, Angelo, said de Ritta had drawn a revolver and fired, the narrative says most of the men in the crowd "seemed eager to take Deritta and lynch him." Police Officer Hutton found him "at the mercy" of men and women who seemed to be trying to tear him to pieces, ordered them back, and hurried him out to Almond Street. Within five minutes a thousand or more people had gathered, many of them shouting for his blood, and Hutton pushed him into the police alarm box at the southeast corner of Fourth and Almond streets and locked the door. The patrol wagon arrived before the crowd could break the box open and took him to the Chestnut Street station.

On October 28 a coroner's jury returned a verdict that the child had been killed by Antonio De Ritta, and he was ordered held for murder. A St. Louis correspondent wrote that de Ritta's wife had also been locked up on a murder charge, and no report of a trial, or of action against anyone in the crowd, appears in the coverage.

Most white papers carried only a one-line wire item about the arrest of a Sicilian rag-picker, with no mention of the crowd, in Minnesota, Ohio, Missouri and Tennessee papers between October 27 and November 2. The full story of the crowd ran in the Wheeling Intelligencer as "A Highly Dramatic Scene in the Discovery of the Murderer" and in the Iron County Register as "Mysterious Murder in St. Louis," both crediting the officer's "prompt action" with saving de Ritta's life. The coverage names the crowd and its target as Italians, and the case drew no Black-press coverage, since that collection begins in 1900.

Accounts differ on the boy's name and age, which also appeared as Valero Robaro, Vevenade Aubno, and Valero Robero, "seventeen years old." A St. Louis letter dated October 27 placed the shooting early that morning and said the boy died in his mother's arms naming "Darita," whereas the longer narrative has him dying instantly and being named by his grandmother and brother.

bases: A crowd of Italian neighbors seized Antonio de Ritta after a boy was shot and, by the papers' account, sought to lynch him until a policeman locked him in a patrol alarm box (A2, A12); no one involved is described as Black.
A crowd of men and women held De Ritta and a throng of a thousand or more shouted for his blood over the alleged killing of the boy, but Officer Hutton got him away and he was not killed (A2, A12).

The shooting and arrest are reported independently by the wire (A1, A3) and a St. Louis letter (A10), but the crowd's attempt on De Ritta appears only in one narrative printed twice (A2, A12); A1 and A10 do not mention it.
